claim: The COVID-19 pandemic is caused by SARS-CoV-2.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic caused by the SARS-CoV-2 has recently emerged as a serious jolt to human life and economy.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about the pandemic.

claim: Initial knowledge established pulmonary complications as the chief symptom of COVID-19.
source: Initial knowledge established pulmonary complications as the chief symptom, however, the neurological aspect of the disease is also becoming increasingly evident.
evidence: This reflects established scientific consensus from early pandemic observations.

claim: The neurological aspect of COVID-19 is becoming increasingly evident.
source: Initial knowledge established pulmonary complications as the chief symptom, however, the neurological aspect of the disease is also becoming increasingly evident.
evidence: This is supported by emerging reports and observations discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has been detected in the CSF of COVID-19 patients.
source: Emerging reports of encephalopathies and similar ailments with the detection of the virus in the CSF has elicited an urgent need for investigating the possibility of neuroinvasiveness of the virus
evidence: This is supported by specific case reports cited later in the manuscript (Moriguchi et al., 2020; Beijing Ditan Hospital, 2020).

claim: ACE2 receptors are expressed at low levels in the brain.
source: the possibility of neuroinvasiveness of the virus, which cannot be ruled out given the expression of low levels of ACE2 receptors in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by the study by Harmer et al., 2002 cited in the manuscript.

claim: Sensory impairments of the olfactory and gustatory systems have been reported in a large proportion of COVID-19 cases.
source: Sensory impairments of the olfactory and gustatory systems have also been reported in a large proportion of the cases, indicating the involvement of the peripheral nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by multiple studies cited in the manuscript (Yan et al., 2020; Vaira et al., 2020; Lechien, 2020).

claim: Sensory impairments in COVID-19 indicate involvement of the peripheral nervous system.
source: Sensory impairments of the olfactory and gustatory systems have also been reported in a large proportion of the cases, indicating the involvement of the peripheral nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of olfactory and gustatory impairments.

claim: The first outbreak of SARS-CoV-2 was reported in the Hubei province of Wuhan.
source: The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), has caused the outbreak of a global pandemic with the first breakout reported in the Hubei province of Wuhan.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the origin of the pandemic.

claim: The clinical manifestation of COVID-19 predominantly involves the respiratory system.
source: Although the clinical manifestation of the COVID-19 disease caused by the virus predominantly involves the respiratory system, recent reports suggest that the pathology of the virus may extend beyond it to involve other organ systems such as the brain and nervous system as well.
evidence: This reflects early clinical observations and established knowledge.

claim: Recent reports suggest that the pathology of SARS-CoV-2 may extend beyond the respiratory system to involve the brain and nervous system.
source: Although the clinical manifestation of the COVID-19 disease caused by the virus predominantly involves the respiratory system, recent reports suggest that the pathology of the virus may extend beyond it to involve other organ systems such as the brain and nervous system as well.
evidence: This is supported by multiple case reports and studies cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Penetration of SARS-CoV-2 into the brain can result in long-term debilitating conditions.
source: Since the penetration of the virus into the brain can result in long-term debilitating conditions, the opportunity for systematic recording of clinical data of such patients to support research efforts should not be missed.
evidence: This is based on inference from neurotropic virus behavior and potential long-term neurological consequences.

claim: ACE2 has been identified as the functional receptor for SARS-CoV-2.
source: The Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) has been identified as the functional receptor for the SARS-CoV-2, which uses its Spike (S) protein C-terminal domain (CTD) to attach to the ACE2 receptor (Wang et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study by Wang et al., 2020a.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 uses its Spike (S) protein C-terminal domain (CTD) to attach to the ACE2 receptor.
source: The Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) has been identified as the functional receptor for the SARS-CoV-2, which uses its Spike (S) protein C-terminal domain (CTD) to attach to the ACE2 receptor (Wang et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study by Wang et al., 2020a.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-CTD has substantially more van der Waals contacts than the receptor binding domain of SARS-CoV.
source: This study showed that the SARS-CoV-2-CTD has substantially more van der Waal contacts than the receptor binding domain of SARS-CoV, and hence exhibits higher binding affinity for ACE2.
evidence: This is data from the Wang et al., 2020a study.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-CTD exhibits higher binding affinity for ACE2 than SARS-CoV.
source: This study showed that the SARS-CoV-2-CTD has substantially more van der Waal contacts than the receptor binding domain of SARS-CoV, and hence exhibits higher binding affinity for ACE2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the increased van der Waals contacts observed in the Wang et al., 2020a study.

claim: Low levels of ACE2 mRNA were detected in the human brain using quantitative real-time RT-PCR.
source: It was observed that although ACE2 was not as ubiquitous as ACE, low levels of ACE2 mRNA were detected in the human brain using quantitative real-time RT-PCR (Harmer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is data from the Harmer et al., 2002 study.

claim: ACE2 protein was expressed abundantly in lung and small intestine tissues.
source: It reported that the ACE2 protein was expressed abundantly in lung and small intestine tissues, and also in venous endothelial and arterial smooth muscles of all organs, including the brain.
evidence: This is data from the Hamming et al., 2004 study.

claim: ACE2 protein was expressed in venous endothelial and arterial smooth muscles of all organs, including the brain.
source: It reported that the ACE2 protein was expressed abundantly in lung and small intestine tissues, and also in venous endothelial and arterial smooth muscles of all organs, including the brain.
evidence: This is data from the Hamming et al., 2004 study.

claim: 36.4% of 214 screened COVID-19 patients displayed some form of neurological symptoms.
source: A preliminary evidence regarding the neurological complications due to the SARS-CoV-2 came from a report from Wuhan, which stated that 36.4% of 214 screened patients of COVID-19 displayed some form of neurological symptoms.
evidence: This is data from the Mao et al., 2020 study.

claim: Out of 214 COVID-19 patients screened, 88 had severe infection.
source: Out of the 214 patients screened, 88 had severe infection and showed higher incidence of the neurological symptoms such as acute cerebrovascular diseases [5.7%] impaired consciousness [14.8%] and skeletal muscle injury [19.3%] (Mao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Mao et al., 2020 study.

claim: Severely infected COVID-19 patients showed higher incidence of neurological symptoms including acute cerebrovascular diseases (5.7%), impaired consciousness (14.8%), and skeletal muscle injury (19.3%).
source: Out of the 214 patients screened, 88 had severe infection and showed higher incidence of the neurological symptoms such as acute cerebrovascular diseases [5.7%] impaired consciousness [14.8%] and skeletal muscle injury [19.3%] (Mao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Mao et al., 2020 study.

claim: A COVID-19 patient in Japan admitted for convulsions accompanied by unconsciousness tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 in a nasopharyngeal swab but had viral RNA detected in the CSF.
source: One study from Japan which described the first case of COVID-19-associated encephalitis where the patient was admitted for convulsions accompanied by unconsciousness reported that although the patient tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 in a nasopharyngeal swab, the viral RNA was surprisingly detected in the CSF, and the patient MRI exhibited abnormalities of the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus (Moriguchi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a case report from Moriguchi et al., 2020.

claim: A COVID-19 patient with encephalitis in Japan had MRI abnormalities of the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus.
source: One study from Japan which described the first case of COVID-19-associated encephalitis where the patient was admitted for convulsions accompanied by unconsciousness reported that although the patient tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 in a nasopharyngeal swab, the viral RNA was surprisingly detected in the CSF, and the patient MRI exhibited abnormalities of the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus (Moriguchi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a case report from Moriguchi et al., 2020.

claim: Viral RNA was detected in the CSF of a COVID-19 patient with encephalopathy in China.
source: A similar report of encephalopathy emerged from China where the viral RNA was also detected in the CSF (Beijing Ditan Hospital, 2020).
evidence: This is a case report from Beijing Ditan Hospital, 2020.

claim: A COVID-19 patient from USA exhibited altered mental status and was diagnosed with acute necrotizing haemorrhagic encephalopathy.
source: It has been reported that a patient from USA, later diagnosed with COVID-19, had exhibited altered mental status. Clinical investigations confirmed acute necrotizing haemorrhagic encephalopathy (Poyiadji et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a case report from Poyiadji et al., 2020.

claim: A COVID-19 patient with acute necrotizing haemorrhagic encephalopathy had brain MRI images showing lesions in the sub-insular regions, thalamus, and medial temporal lobes.
source: Since the CSF was limited, SARS-CoV-2 analysis could not be performed but the brain MRI images showed lesions in the sub-insular regions, and the thalamus and medial temporal lobes.
evidence: This is data from the Poyiadji et al., 2020 case report.

claim: An elderly COVID-19 patient from Iran suffered a severe intracerebral haemorrhage and was presented unconscious.
source: An elderly patient from Iran, who tested positive to COVID-19, had suffered a severe intracerebral haemorrhage and was presented unconscious. (Sharifi-Razavi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a case report from Sharifi-Razavi et al., 2020.

claim: A correlation exists between COVID-19 patients and concomitant encephalopathy and cerebropathy observed without any obvious cause other than the viral infection.
source: It appears that a correlation exists between COVID-19 patients and the concomitant encephalopathy and cerebropathy observed without any obvious cause other than the viral infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the multiple case reports presented.

claim: A COVID-19 patient with Parkinson's Disease presented with focal dysfunction of the left temporal lobe and altered mental status.
source: There is also a report of a COVID-19 patient with Parkinson's Disease who presented with focal dysfunction of the left temporal lobe and altered mental status (Filatov et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a case report from Filatov et al., 2020.

claim: Pre-existing disorders of the nervous system may play a role in exacerbating the neurological aspect of COVID-19 and may be a risk factor for increased pulmonary complications.
source: This raises the question whether pre-existing disorders of the nervous system may play a role in exacerbating the neurological aspect of the disease and may be a risk factor for increased pulmonary complications.
evidence: This is speculation based on the case of a patient with Parkinson's Disease.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may lead to an increase in the incidence of neurodegenerative disorders in affected individuals in the future.
source: On the other hand, it will also be interesting to know whether SARS-CoV-2 leads to an increase in the incidence of neurodegenerative disorders in the affected individuals in the future (De Felice, 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about potential long-term consequences, with a citation to De Felice, 2019.

claim: Hypoxic injury to the brain caused by respiratory failure in COVID-19 patients is of serious concern.
source: Nevertheless, hypoxic injury to the brain caused by respiratory failure in COVID-19 patients is of serious concern.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of respiratory failure consequences and supported by the following data.

claim: Hypoxic encephalopathy was reported in 20% of 113 deceased COVID-19 patients in China.
source: In this context, hypoxic encephalopathy was reported in 20% of 113 deceased COVID-19 patients in China (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Chen et al., 2020 study.

claim: A study from the National Hospital in London examined data from 43 SARS-CoV-2 positive patients who exhibited neurological problems.
source: Recently, a detailed study carried out by a multidisciplinary group from the National Hospital in London, examined data from SARS-CoV-2 positive patients who exhibited neurological problems. The clinical, radiological, laboratory and neuropathological findings of 43 qualifying patients were studied retrospectively by the team.
evidence: This is data from the Paterson et al., 2020 study.

claim: In the London study, neurological complications in COVID-19 patients included encephalopathies (10/43), inflammatory CNS syndromes (12/43), ischaemic stroke (8/43), peripheral neurological disorders (8/43), and miscellaneous central disorders (5/43).
source: The categories of neurological complications included encephalopathies (10/43), inflammatory CNS syndromes (12/43), ischaemic stroke (8/43), peripherical neurological disorders (8/43) and miscellaneous central disorders (5/43) (Paterson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Paterson et al., 2020 study.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may be capable of inflicting injury to the brain in different ways.
source: Thus, reports such as these, suggest that the SARS-CoV-2 may be capable of inflicting injury to the brain in different ways.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variety of neurological complications reported.

claim: In a study at Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, 449 severe COVID-19 patients were recruited from among 1786 consecutive patients to study coagulopathy-associated stroke.
source: In Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, 449 severe COVID-19 patients were recruited from among 1786 consecutive patients to study coagulopathy-associated stroke.
evidence: This is data from the Tang et al., 2020 study.

claim: Administering heparin to severe COVID-19 patients with sepsis-induced coagulopathy and elevated D-dimer levels resulted in better prognosis.
source: The study used sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC) along with elevated D-dimer levels to show that administering heparin to severe COVID-19 patients resulted in better prognosis (Tang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Tang et al., 2020 study.

claim: Acute cerebrovascular diseases was reported in 5.7% of patients with severe COVID-19 infection.
source: In the study by Mao et al., 2020, acute cerebrovascular diseases was reported in 5.7% patients with severe infection.
evidence: This is data from the Mao et al., 2020 study.

claim: In a study with 219 COVID-19 patients, 10 (4.6%) suffered from ischaemic stroke and 1 (0.5%) had developed intracerebral haemorrhage.
source: Another study with 219 COVID-19 patients found that 10 (4.6%) suffered from ischaemic stroke and 1 (0.5%) had developed intracerebral haemorrhage.
evidence: This is data from the Li et al., 2020 study.

claim: COVID-19 stroke patients showed higher levels of inflammatory markers like C-Reactive Protein and D-dimer.
source: The stroke patients also showed higher levels of inflammatory markers like C-Reactive Protein and D-dimer (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Li et al., 2020 study.

claim: Six COVID-19 patients at National Hospital, London who suffered from ischaemic stroke presented with large vessel occlusion and elevated D-dimer levels (>1000 μL).
source: Elevated D-dimer levels (>1000 μL) were also reported in the study at National Hospital, London where six COVID-19 patients who suffered from ischaemic stroke presented with large vessel occlusion (Beyrouti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Beyrouti et al., 2020 study.

claim: COVID-19 patients with ischaemic stroke exhibited higher levels of ferritin and lactate dehydrogenase usually reported in severe cases.
source: These patients also exhibited higher levels of ferritin and lactate dehydrogenase usually reported in severe cases.
evidence: This is data from the Beyrouti et al., 2020 study.

claim: COVID-19 infection was linked to a prothrombic state conducive to stroke.
source: Although a causal relationship between COVID-19 and ischaemic stroke could not be confirmed because of competing conditions, the infection was linked to the prothrombic state conducive to stroke.
evidence: This is an inference from the Beyrouti et al., 2020 study.

claim: A retrospective study examined radiological evidence of 4 COVID-19 patients and attributed the cerebrovascular accident to likely hypercoagulability with elevated D-dimer.
source: Another retrospective study examined the radiological evidence of 4 patients and attributed the cerebrovascular accident to likely hypercoagulability; elevated D-dimer was also reported in these cases (Avula et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Avula et al., 2020 study.

claim: Records of 3556 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in the New York metropolitan area were inducted in a retrospective study, with data from 32 patients having proven ischaemic stroke analyzed.
source: Records of 3556 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in the New York metropolitan area were inducted in a retrospective study. Among these, the data from 32 patients having proven ischaemic stroke was analysed.
evidence: This is data from the Yaghi et al., 2020 study.

claim: A majority of strokes in COVID-19 patients in the New York study were cryptogenic and correlated to acquired hypercoagulability.
source: A majority of the strokes reported in this study were cryptogenic and correlated to acquired hypercoagulability (Yaghi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Yaghi et al., 2020 study.

claim: It is still a matter of debate if COVID-19-related strokes are a direct cause of viral infection to the cerebrovascular system.
source: However, it is still a matter of debate if these strokes are a direct cause of viral infection to the cerebrovascular system.
evidence: This reflects the current state of scientific uncertainty on the mechanism.

claim: Smell and taste loss were experienced in 68% and 71% of 59 COVID-19 positive patients, respectively.
source: A recent study reported that smell and taste loss were experienced in 68% and 71% of 59 COVID‐19 positive patients, respectively.
evidence: This is data from the Yan et al., 2020 study.

claim: Smell and taste impairments were ten times more likely in ambulatory COVID-19 positive patients.
source: It was observed that these impairments were ten times more likely in ambulatory COVID‐19 positive patients.
evidence: This is data from the Yan et al., 2020 study.

claim: Spontaneous improvement in smell and taste symptoms was observed in a majority of COVID-19 cases which correlated well with clinical recovery.
source: Fortunately, spontaneous improvement in these symptoms was observed in a majority of the cases which correlated well with the clinical recovery (Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Yan et al., 2020 study.

claim: A study from Italy reported chemosensitive symptoms in 73.6% of 72 COVID-19 patients treated at the University Hospital of Sassari.
source: One study from Italy reported these chemosensitive symptoms in 73.6% of 72 patients treated at the University Hospital of Sassari (Vaira et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Vaira et al., 2020 study.

claim: A multicenter European study involving 417 COVID-19 patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms and mean age 36.9 ± 11.4 years reported olfactory and gustatory impairments in 85.6% and 88.0% of patients, respectively.
source: Another independent multicenter European study involving 417 COVID-19 patients, with mild-to-moderate symptoms and mean age 36.9 ± 11.4 years, reported olfactory and gustatory impairments in 85.6% and 88.0% of patients, respectively.
evidence: This is data from the Lechien, 2020 study.

claim: Females were more likely to develop COVID-19 associated anosmia and ageusia as compared to males.
source: Interestingly, this study found that females were more likely to develop COVID-19 associated anosmia and ageusia as compared to males, although the reason for this is unclear (Lechien, 2020).
evidence: This is data from the Lechien, 2020 study.

claim: Olfactory and gustatory dysfunctions were more prevalent among European COVID-19 patients.
source: Also, these dysfunctions were more prevalent among European patients.
evidence: This is data from the Lechien, 2020 study.

claim: Anosmia and ageusia are early symptoms of COVID-19 infection.
source: Clinical observations across countries have put on record that anosmia and ageusia are early symptoms of COVID-19 infection (Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple clinical observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: Viruses in general, and SARS-CoV-2 in particular, can infect peripheral neurons and subsequently gain access to the CNS.
source: It may be well argued that viruses in general, and SARS-COV-2 in particular, can infect peripheral neurons and subsequently gain access to the CNS.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of viral neurotropism and inference from the observed symptoms.

claim: SARS-CoV was present in the cerebrum of four fatal SARS patient samples.
source: The four fatal SARS patient samples had shown the presence of SARS-CoV in the cerebrum, establishing neurotropic behaviour of the virus.
evidence: This is data from a previous study on SARS-CoV organ distribution.

claim: The presence of SARS-CoV in the cerebrum establishes neurotropic behaviour of the virus.
source: The four fatal SARS patient samples had shown the presence of SARS-CoV in the cerebrum, establishing neurotropic behaviour of the virus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the detection of virus in brain tissue.

claim: Both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 mediate host cell entry through ACE2 receptor.
source: Since both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 mediate host cell entry through ACE2 receptor, the presence of SARS-CoV-2 in the CSF of some patients is troubling and suggests the possibility of neuroinvasive potential of the virus
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of viral entry.

claim: The presence of SARS-CoV-2 in the CSF of some patients suggests the possibility of neuroinvasive potential of the virus.
source: Since both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 mediate host cell entry through ACE2 receptor, the presence of SARS-CoV-2 in the CSF of some patients is troubling and suggests the possibility of neuroinvasive potential of the virus
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the detection of virus in CSF and comparison with SARS-CoV.

claim: Viremia has been reported in the case of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Viremia has been reported in the case of SARS-CoV-2 and it is possible that the virus may be able to spread hematogenously and breach the blood-brain barrier due to the cytokine storm reported as a pathology (Hirano and Murakami, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Hirano and Murakami, 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may be able to spread hematogenously and breach the blood-brain barrier due to the cytokine storm.
source: Viremia has been reported in the case of SARS-CoV-2 and it is possible that the virus may be able to spread hematogenously and breach the blood-brain barrier due to the cytokine storm reported as a pathology (Hirano and Murakami, 2020).
evidence: This is speculation based on known viremia and cytokine storm pathology.

claim: ACE2 receptors present on the capillary endothelium may facilitate SARS-CoV-2 entry into the CNS.
source: The ACE2 receptors present on the capillary endothelium may facilitate this process.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of ACE2 on endothelium and the virus's use of ACE2 for entry.

claim: Besides the ACE2 receptor, SARS-CoV-2 uses TMPRSS2 as well as endosomal cysteine proteases to assist S-protein binding.
source: Although the exact route of entry into the CNS still remains unclear, Hoffmann et al., 2020 have demonstrated that besides the ACE2 receptor, SARS-CoV-2 uses TMPRSS2 as well as endosomal cysteine proteases to assist S-protein binding.
evidence: This is data from the Hoffmann et al., 2020 study.

claim: The neurotropic transgression most likely occurs via olfactory aspiration.
source: The neurotropic transgression most likely occurs via olfactory aspiration.
evidence: This is speculation based on anatomical considerations and supported by animal model data.

claim: The brain was a major target organ of SARS-CoV in mice transgenic for the human ACE2 receptor.
source: For instance, the brain was a major target organ of SARS-CoV in mice transgenic for the human ACE2 receptor (Tseng et al., 2007), and the virus infected the brain via the olfactory bulb, spreading quickly to the other parts by extensive neuronal infection (Netland et al., 2008).
evidence: This is data from the Tseng et al., 2007 study.

claim: SARS-CoV infected the brain via the olfactory bulb in transgenic mice, spreading quickly to other parts by extensive neuronal infection.
source: For instance, the brain was a major target organ of SARS-CoV in mice transgenic for the human ACE2 receptor (Tseng et al., 2007), and the virus infected the brain via the olfactory bulb, spreading quickly to the other parts by extensive neuronal infection (Netland et al., 2008).
evidence: This is data from the Netland et al., 2008 study.

claim: The anatomy of the nasal cavity and its proximity to the forebrain may act as a route of entry for SARS-CoV-2.
source: This is understandable, given the anatomy of the nasal cavity and its proximity to the forebrain, which may act as a route of entry for the virus (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: If SARS-CoV-2 breaches the blood-brain-barrier and disseminates into the brain tissue, its spread will probably be mediated by the recruitment of pathways with specific neurotransmitters across the cerebrum.
source: If the virus breaches the blood-brain-barrier and disseminates into the brain tissue, its spread will probably be mediated by the recruitment of pathways with specific neurotransmitters across the cerebrum.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of viral spread in the brain.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 can spread via neuronal retrograde mechanism where it invades peripheral neurons but ultimately gains entry to the brain and CNS by spreading through the connected network of neuronal transport machinery.
source: The virus can also spread via neuronal retrograde mechanism where it invades the peripheral neurons but ultimately gains entry to the brain and CNS by spreading through the connected network of neuronal transport machinery (Zhou et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Zhou et al., 2020b.

claim: The possibility of SARS-CoV-2 neuroinvasion via the enteric pathway has come to light, suggesting the virus may prime the enteric nervous system or reach the CNS via intestinal vagal afferents.
source: Recently, the possibility of neuroinvasion via the enteric pathway has also come to light which suggests that the virus may prime the enteric nervous system or reach the CNS via intestinal vagal afferents (Esposito et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Esposito et al., 2020.

claim: The effects of SARS-CoV-2 neuroinvasion can be debilitating in some severe cases.
source: Whatever maybe the route of neuroinvasion, it is clear that the effects can be debilitating in some severe cases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the severe neurological complications reported.

claim: Neurodegenerative disorders sometimes take more than a decade to manifest.
source: Another consideration is that since neurodegenerative disorders sometimes take more than a decade to manifest, the long-term pathophysiological outcomes of the SARS-CoV-2 neurotropism should be considered as a matter of serious concern by researchers in this field.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neurodegenerative disease progression.

claim: The long-term pathophysiological outcomes of SARS-CoV-2 neurotropism should be considered as a matter of serious concern.
source: Another consideration is that since neurodegenerative disorders sometimes take more than a decade to manifest, the long-term pathophysiological outcomes of the SARS-CoV-2 neurotropism should be considered as a matter of serious concern by researchers in this field.
evidence: This is an inference based on the potential for delayed neurological consequences.

claim: Studies on transgenic rodent models expressing human ACE2 receptors unravelled the mechanisms of SARS-CoV neurotropism.
source: Earlier, some studies on the transgenic rodent models, which expressed human ACE2 receptors, had unravelled the mechanisms of SARS-CoV neurotropism (Tseng et al., 2007; Netland et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tseng et al., 2007 and Netland et al., 2008.

claim: There is no clear evidence of how SARS-CoV-2 mediates neuroinvasion.
source: However, the fact that there is no clear evidence of how the virus mediates neuroinvasion, leaves the door open to probe this question with the help of animal models.
evidence: This reflects the current state of knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 neuroinvasion mechanisms.

claim: Whether or not SARS-CoV-2 can use the low levels of ACE2 receptors in the brain to infect neurons needs to be investigated.
source: Whether or not the virus can use the low levels of ACE2 receptors in the brain to infect the neurons needs to be investigated.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: SARS-CoV-2's ability to thrive and replicate in the CSF needs to be examined thoroughly.
source: Also, since the virus has been detected in the CSF of many COVID-19 patients, its ability to thrive and replicate in the CSF needs to be examined thoroughly.
evidence: This identifies a research need based on the detection of virus in CSF.

claim: The possible effects of SARS-CoV-2 on different parts of the brain, spinal cord and peripheral nervous system should be evaluated.
source: The possible effects of the virus on different parts of the brain, spinal cord and peripheral nervous system should also be evaluated so that the pathophysiology behind the neurological symptoms observed in patients can be understood in greater detail.
evidence: This identifies a research need to understand neurological pathophysiology.

claim: Diagnostic procedures for COVID-19 should include neurodiagnostic tests in cases where neurological symptoms are observed.
source: As the clinicians are becoming increasingly aware of the neurological complications due to SARS-CoV-2, the diagnostic procedures should not be solely focused around the pulmonary manifestations, but include neurodiagnostic tests in cases where neurological symptoms are observed.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the emerging evidence of neurological complications.

claim: The RNA of SARS-CoV-2 particles isolated from CSF or post-mortem brain tissue samples should be sequenced for phylogenetic analysis to identify possible tissue-specific compartmentalization.
source: The RNA of the virus particles isolated from the CSF or post-mortem brain tissue samples should also be sequenced so that phylogenetic analysis can shed light on the possibility of any tissue-specific compartmentalization of the virus.
evidence: This is a proposed research approach to investigate viral compartmentalization.

claim: The manifestation of Guillain-Barré syndrome in some COVID-19 patients hints at possible immune system disruptions caused by the virus.
source: Furthermore, since the manifestation of Guillain-Barré syndrome in some COVID-19 patients also hints at possible immune system disruptions caused by the virus, the effect of the virus on the neuroimmune system should be thoroughly investigated.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of Guillain-Barré syndrome in COVID-19 patients.

claim: The effect of SARS-CoV-2 on the neuroimmune system should be thoroughly investigated.
source: Furthermore, since the manifestation of Guillain-Barré syndrome in some COVID-19 patients also hints at possible immune system disruptions caused by the virus, the effect of the virus on the neuroimmune system should be thoroughly investigated.
evidence: This is a research recommendation based on observed immune-related neurological complications.

claim: The pulmonary aspect of COVID-19 is largely known and accepted.
source: The pulmonary aspect of the disease is largely known and accepted but due to the recently emerged possibility of its neuro-invasive nature, several unanswered questions have surfaced.
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge at the time of writing.

claim: Autopsies of deceased COVID-19 patients and thorough examination of brain and spinal cord tissues may shed light on neuroinvasion.
source: Autopsies of deceased patients and thorough examination of the brain and spinal cord tissues may shed some light on this topic.
evidence: This is a proposed research approach.

claim: Probing the CSF for the presence of viral RNA may provide a better picture of SARS-CoV-2's mechanisms of invasion.
source: Moreover, probing the CSF for the presence of viral RNA, whenever possible or suspected may provide a better picture of its mechanisms of invasion.
evidence: This is a proposed diagnostic and research approach.

claim: There is an immediate need to carry out experimental studies involving animal models to investigate possible mechanisms by which SARS-CoV-2 can gain entry into the brain and cause deleterious effects on the nervous system.
source: As the neurological aspect of the viral infection remains very poorly understood, there is an immediate need to carry out experimental studies involving animal models of the disease to investigate the possible mechanisms by which the virus can gain entry into the brain, as well as cause deleterious effects on the nervous system.
evidence: This is a research recommendation based on gaps in current understanding.

claim: Figure 1 depicts possible routes of SARS-CoV-2 neuroinvasion including hematogenous spread and neuronal retrograde spread.
source: The possible routes of neuroinvasion have been depicted in Figure 1.
evidence: The figure illustrates multiple pathways including infection through blood-brain barrier breach, microvascular endothelial cells, olfactory nerves, and enteric nervous system.
